blocks.html: ⛵ Discovering Opportunities On Your Own.
Personally embarking on an active search for a role is often the most straightforward approach, and will likely be the first port of call for those looking for a new opportunity.
How to find new roles.
Typically, you will discover the existence of open roles through one of two main methods:
Through a 'job board', composed of openings currently on offer from multiple studios.

Through finding a company first, and looking for any relevant roles to which you might be suited.
One fun way way to discover studios you might enjoy working with is to play a lot of games, and see which developers create the type of content you could see yourself working on.
You can find company listings, as well as public job boards at ‣.

Keep in mind that there exists a vast underground of 'unlisted' positions in the industry, so if there is somewhere you are really keen to work, you should always send in what is commonly called a 'speculative' or 'open' application. Most studios will have an indication on their careers page on how to do this. If they don't, feel free to enquire via their publically-available contact methods (bearing in mind that you will likely not hear back).

🕸️ Networking.
Another method of coming across opportunities is to leverage the collective power of professional networks.
General Guidelines.
The good news is that if you are here, you are already part of an absolutely incredibly welcoming network of people from around the world.
If you're looking for a new opportunity, the #job-listings channels on the We Can Fix It In UI Discord can be a great place to start!

There are numerous ways to approach networking, both online and offline. However, no matter which medium you select, with as much pressure as there likely is to secure a job quickly, it is critical to not approach 'networking' with the mentality of a job-hunter. Making an approach in such a predatory fashion can both be incredibly discourteous, highly uncomfortable, and will always result in the opposite of the desired outcome.

It goes without saying that it is absolutely essential to practice the highest degree of empathy and respect towards others when being granted access to a network. It is important to remember that nobody owes you anything, and repeated nagging, and especially harassment of any kind will not be tolerated. The industry is relatively small, and a bad reputation within a network and its members will not do you any favours in your pursuits.

Instead of coming in with blinders on, solely focused on generating results, networking should instead be approached with an attitude of finding enjoyment in getting to meet and spend time with people who share the same passions (and perhaps even struggles) as you. Just as making a new friend, establishing rapport with the members of your new tribe will take some time. By the time you receive a lead from an individual in your network, it should feel like a trusted, personal gesture from someone who cares about you as their peer, and wants you to find success.

Generally speaking, an opportunity from a network will come in the form of your peer performing an 'introduction' to a person with jurisdiciton over, or more knowledge of, an opening. From there, you will have the opportunity to learn more, and find if there is a potential fit.
Network referrals are especially good for the following reasons:
They can generally be trusted as authentic, and 'available'.
If this is not a publicly listed ('underground') opportunity, competition will be far lower (or even potentially non-existent).
You will typically be able to completely bypass a company's 'full' application process, and be put directly in contact with someone with jurisdiction over the opening.
You might be able to completely skip parts of ‣.
Through being referred by a mutual contact in your network, you will automatically gain a point of endorsement for, at the minimum, being an individual of good repute.
Not sure where to find your tribe? You can find a varied selection of groups to join under ‣.
🕵️ Recruiters & Headhunters.
A Primer on Recruiters and Recruitment Techniques.
The more experience you accrue, the more often you will be approached by studio Recruiters, or third-party 'Headhunters'.

A mistake those new to the recruitment game often make is confounding expressed interest by a recruiter or company, as being offered a position. This is never the case.
In fact, a lot of recruitment tactics involve a 'shotgun' approach, where as many candidates who appear as if they might have a relevant background will be contacted as a 'feeler' to see who responds. From those that respond, recruiters will then strive to learn just enough to determine whether it is worth inviting the person in question to the first phase of ‣, from where further determinations can be made.

In almost all cases, recruiters will find you, and contact you via LinkedIn. With that said if you are open to being 'headhunted', you should absolutely consider creating a professional LinkedIn account, and keeping it up-to-date.

Considerations for Accepting the Services of a Recruiter.
The biggest reasons to accept the help of any type of recruiter are that:
They will do most of the heavy lifting of searching for jobs that are a potential fit to what you have to offer.

In a lot of cases, being headhunted represents a show of interest in you, so you will sometimes be able to dispense with Cover Letters, lengthy online forms, and any other formalities typically sprinkled in to add friction to applications from the general public.
If you are being approached by a studio or hybrid recruiter, you will have no choice but to work with them to proceed to the next phase of ‣.

A lot of the disadvantages, on the other hand, are usually a result of incredible pressure applied to many working in recruiting. This is especially visible in the low-barrier-to-entry, but ultra-competitive field of third-party headhunting, where mercenaries will often cut corners, and employ certain cut-throat tactics which will not always be to the benefit of the applicant, or the company looking to hire.
Great opportunities can be found, but always proceed with vigilance.

Some studio recruiters and headhunters engage in the practice of performing unscheduled calls, either because it's convenient for them, or as a technique to catch you off guard. This is hugely unprofessional on their part, and you have every right to tell them that you are not available (what you're doing is none of their business) and that you would be happy to talk at a time that you both schedule together. (This could be as early as within the hour, or at some point over the following days).
